segments.text: There's a deep-sea animal that builds an entire house out of its own snot. Then it just walks away.
The animal itself? Two inches long. Doesn't even have a mouth you'd recognize.

vis.prompt: Extreme close-up of a small translucent tadpole-shaped deep-sea animal, delicate internal organs faintly visible through its gelatinous body, a simple tail and basic feeding structure, suspended in dark water illuminated by a single research light, realistic deep-sea documentary photography style, scientifically accurate anatomy

segments.text: But the house — pure mucus, up to three feet wide — is bigger than the room you're sitting in.

vis.prompt: A wide dramatic deep-sea shot showing a giant translucent mucus filter structure floating next to a human diver silhouette in full scuba gear, positioned so the diver's height clearly shows the structure is roughly three times taller than the diver, dark abyssal water, illuminated by a diving light, realistic deep-sea documentary photography style, clear unambiguous size comparison, emphasizing enormous scale

segments.text: It's not for living in. It's a filter. Every particle drifting past gets caught before it reaches the animal's actual mouth.

segments.text: And it clogs — every single day — so the animal abandons the whole house and builds a brand new one from scratch.

segments.text: That abandoned mucus doesn't just disappear. It sinks — fast, almost a kilometer a day — straight to the ocean floor.

segments.text: Multiply that by every larvacean in the ocean, and you've got one of the planet's biggest carbon pumps — built entirely out of snot nobody wanted.
